---
title: "Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia"
---

*Status: first published indicator (milestone M3 in progress). Regenerate
with `uv run sohbc build mortality_rates_bc`.*

This is the project's first end-to-end
[indicator](../reference/index.qmd): it is fetched from a catalogued
source, tidied by the pipeline, and published as a versioned dataset plus
the views below. Each indicator page states its provenance and caveats
(see the [roadmap](../ROADMAP.md), milestone M3).

## Provenance

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Domain** | [Mortality](../reference/measurement-framework.qmd) |
| **Definition** | Deaths and the mortality rate (deaths per 1,000 population), all ages, by sex (both sexes, males, females), resident in British Columbia; crude and directly age-standardised per sex (WHO World Standard Population 2000–2025) [@whoStandardPop] |
| **Source** | Statistics Canada, table 13-10-0710-01, *Mortality rates, by age group* [@statcan_wds_table] |
| **Access** | Statistics Canada Web Data Service (automated full-table download) |
| **Form** | indicator table (published summary statistics) |
| **Geography** | British Columbia, place of residence |
| **Coverage** | 1991–present (annual); observation window shown on each figure |
| **Frequency / refresh** | annual |
| **Licence** | Statistics Canada Open Licence |
| **Proxy note** | A proxy for the mortality domain, not the state of health itself ([why](../explanation/definition-of-health.qmd#proxies-are-not-the-state-of-health)) |

## Trend

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
rows = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv").csv({typed: true})
rates = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.age_group === "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.sex === "Both sexes")
bySexRates = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.age_group === "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.sex !== "Both sexes")
counts = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Number of deaths" && d.sex === "Both sexes")
asr = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv").csv({typed: true}).filter(d => d.sex === "Both sexes")
bySexAsr = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv").csv({typed: true}).filter(d => d.sex !== "Both sexes")
trend = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json").json()
asrTrend = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json").json()
bySexTrend = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json").json()
series = rates.map(d => ({year: d.ref_date, rate: d.value, series: "Crude"}))
  .concat(asr.map(d => ({year: d.ref_date, rate: d.value, series: "Age-standardised"})))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Mortality rate, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([{x1: 2020, x2: 2025}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "grey", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX(trend.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(asrTrend.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(series, {x: "year", y: "rate", stroke: "series", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(series, {x: "year", y: "rate", stroke: "series", tip: true})
  ]
})
```

The **crude** rate is per 1,000 residents at the observed age mix; the
**age-standardised** rate applies the WHO World Standard Population
(2000–2025) [@whoStandardPop], removing the effect of BC's ageing
population. The grey band marks the COVID-19 period (2020–2024); the red
dashed lines are the crude rate's regime breaks, the blue dotted lines
the age-standardised rate's.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Number of deaths, British Columbia",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths"},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(counts, {x: "ref_date", y: "value"}),
    Plot.dot(counts, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", tip: true})
  ]
})
```

## Trajectory and regimes

Trend summaries, recomputed on every build
(`data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json`,
`data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json`):

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
segments = trend.segments.length
  ? trend.segments
  : [{label: "whole series", start: trend.start, end: trend.end, ...trend.overall}]
Inputs.table(segments, {
  columns: ["label", "start", "end", "slope_per_year", "slope_per_decade", "fitted_start", "fitted_end", "change_within"],
  header: {label: "crude segment", start: "from", end: "to", slope_per_year: "slope/yr", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", fitted_start: "level at start", fitted_end: "level at end", change_within: "change within"}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
jumpRows = trend.jumps.length
  ? trend.jumps.map(j => ({year: j.year, previous_level: j.previous_level, next_level: j.next_level, jump: j.jump}))
  : [{year: "—", previous_level: "—", next_level: "—", jump: 0}]
Inputs.table(jumpRows, {
  columns: ["year", "previous_level", "next_level", "jump"],
  header: {year: "break", previous_level: "level before", next_level: "level after", jump: "level jump"}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
dc = trend.decomposition
md`The break at **${trend.change_point}** is mostly a change of
**slope**, not of level: the total change of
${dc.observed_change.toFixed(2)} decomposes into
${dc.within_regime_change.toFixed(2)} within the regimes and
${dc.between_regime_change.toFixed(2)} in level jumps at the breaks.`
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Over ${trend.start}–${trend.end} the crude rate changed by
**${trend.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** per 1,000 per decade, and the
series is **${trend.stationarity.verdict}**.
It carries a monotone trend (Kendall's tau = ${trend.trend_test.tau.toFixed(2)},
p = ${trend.trend_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}) and departure from a single straight
line (residual-permutation test, p = ${trend.break_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}).
The BIC-selected regimes break at ${trend.change_points.join(", ")}, the largest
slope change at **${trend.change_point}**${trend.change_point === 2020 ? " — the onset of the COVID-19 period" : ""}.`
```

The age-standardised rate tells a different story, because it is the one
that abstracts from population ageing:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
asrSegments = asrTrend.segments
Inputs.table(asrSegments, {
  columns: ["label", "start", "end", "slope_per_year", "slope_per_decade"],
  header: {label: "standardised segment", start: "from", end: "to", slope_per_year: "slope/yr", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade"}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`The age-standardised rate is **${asrTrend.stationarity.verdict}**
(Kendall's tau = ${asrTrend.trend_test.tau.toFixed(2)},
p = ${asrTrend.trend_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}; break test
p = ${asrTrend.break_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}), with a regime break at
**${asrTrend.change_point}**: the decline reverses there — the standardised
rate fell before it and has risen since.`
```

**Method.** Regimes are dated by a piecewise-linear segmentation, solved
exactly by dynamic programming, with the number of breaks chosen by BIC;
whether the series departs from one straight line is tested by residual
permutation [@truong2020selective], and the trend by Kendall's tau. Each
series is therefore labelled stationary or not over its observed window,
as milestone M3 requires. The full test output, including every candidate
segmentation, is in the trend JSON. The permutation test assumes
exchangeable residuals — autocorrelation is not modelled — so it is a
test of departure from a linear trend, not a full time-series model.

## Sex breakdown

The source table publishes males and females separately; both are built
through the same pipeline, including per-sex age standardisation, and
each carries its own stationarity verdict
(`data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json`).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Crude mortality rate by sex, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.crude.Males.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.lineY(bySexRates, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(bySexRates, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Age-standardised mortality rate by sex, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.age_standardised.Males.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.age_standardised.Females.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(bySexAsr, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(bySexAsr, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sexRows = ["Males", "Females"].flatMap(sex => [
  {series: "Crude", sex, ...bySexTrend.crude[sex]},
  {series: "Age-standardised", sex, ...bySexTrend.age_standardised[sex]}
]).map(d => ({
  series: d.series,
  sex: d.sex,
  slope_per_decade: d.overall.slope_per_decade,
  verdict: d.stationarity.verdict,
  change_points: d.change_points.join(", ") || "—",
  change_point: d.change_point ?? "—"
}))
Inputs.table(sexRows, {
  columns: ["series", "sex", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "change_points", "change_point"],
  header: {series: "series", sex: "sex", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", verdict: "stationarity", change_points: "regime breaks", change_point: "largest break"}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`Every sex-specific series is nonstationary over ${bySexTrend.crude.Males.start}–${bySexTrend.crude.Males.end}.
Males sit above females on both crude and standardised rates throughout, and
the standardised decline-then-reversal appears in both sexes, but the
standardised turnaround is dated **${bySexTrend.age_standardised.Males.change_point}**
for males and **${bySexTrend.age_standardised.Females.change_point}** for females —
close to, but not identical with, the both-sexes date of
${asrTrend.change_point}; the sexes should be read as separate trajectories,
not one trend disaggregated after the fact.`
```

## Age breakdown

The same source carries every five-year age group. Each is built into its
own trajectory, so we can ask whether the decline is general or driven by
particular ages (`data/published/mortality_age_specific_bc_by_age_trend.json`;
generated by `uv run sohbc build mortality_age_specific_bc`).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
byAge = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_age_specific_bc_by_age_trend.json").json()
ageRows = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.sex === "Both sexes" && d.age_group !== "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.age_group !== "Age at time of death, not stated")
ageOrder = ["under 1 year", "1 to 4 years", "5 to 9 years", "10 to 14 years", "15 to 19 years", "20 to 24 years", "25 to 29 years", "30 to 34 years", "35 to 39 years", "40 to 44 years", "45 to 49 years", "50 to 54 years", "55 to 59 years", "60 to 64 years", "65 to 69 years", "70 to 74 years", "75 to 79 years", "80 to 84 years", "85 to 89 years", "90 years and over"]
short = g => g.replace("Age at time of death, ", "")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  title: "Mortality rate by age group, both sexes (per 1,000; 5-year bands)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {label: null, domain: ageOrder.slice().reverse()},
  color: {scheme: "YlGnBu", legend: true, label: "per 1,000"},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(ageRows, {x: "ref_date", y: d => short(d.age_group), fill: "value", tip: true})
  ],
  width: 900
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ageSummary = ageOrder.map(g => {
  const t = byAge["Both sexes"][`Age at time of death, ${g}`]
  return t && {
    age: g,
    slope_per_decade: t.overall.slope_per_decade,
    verdict: t.stationarity.verdict,
    change_point: t.change_point ?? "—"
  }
}).filter(Boolean)
Inputs.table(ageSummary, {
  columns: ["age", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "change_point"],
  header: {age: "age group", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade (per 1,000)", verdict: "stationarity", change_point: "largest break"}
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
oldest = byAge["Both sexes"]["Age at time of death, 90 years and over"]
youngest = byAge["Both sexes"]["Age at time of death, 30 to 34 years"]
md`The decline is real at **every** age, but its size scales with age:
about **${oldest.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(1)}** per 1,000 per decade
at 90 and over, against roughly **${youngest.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}**
at 30–34. The all-ages crude rate discussed above mixes these: an ageing
population shifts weight toward the high-rate old groups, so the all-ages
crude rate can rise even while every age-specific rate falls. This is the
same ageing signature seen in the crude-versus-standardised contrast,
decomposed by age.`
```

**Method.** Each age group is summarised by the same
:func:`~sohbc.indicators.trajectory` routine as the headline series
(piecewise-linear regimes by BIC, residual-permutation break test,
Kendall-tau trend). Because there are 20 groups, the age-specific build
uses 199 permutations rather than the headline 1,999; this coarsens the
p-value but not the regime dating. Small counts in the youngest groups
make their rates volatile, so their slopes and breaks are weakly
identified.

## Caveats

- **Crude vs standardised.** Two series are published: the crude rate
  (observed age mix) and a directly age-standardised rate using the WHO
  World Standard Population (2000–2025) [@whoStandardPop]. The crude rate
  can rise while the standardised rate falls if the population ages — seen
  here, so read the two together.
- **Break detection, not explanation.** The regimes are dated by a formal
  test (above) [@truong2020selective]; the test says that a break beyond a
  single straight line exists, not what caused it, and the 2020–2024
  regime rests on five annual points, so its slope is the least certain.
- **The standardised turnaround predates the pandemic.** The
  age-standardised rate's regime break falls at 2013, before the COVID-19
  period, so the pandemic does not explain the reversal on its own; the
  pipeline dates the change and does not attribute it.
- **Observation window and regimes.** The series spans 1991–2024 and
  crosses the COVID-19 period (2020–2024), marked on the figure.
- **Sex categories are the source's.** The table publishes both sexes,
  males, and females; the pipeline reports these categories as given and
  does not model sex or gender beyond them.
- **Resolution.** Published at provincial resolution, with age-group rows
  (both sexes) and male/female breakdowns in the tidy file, and
  age-specific trajectories in a separate summary. Sub-provincial views
  are a separate indicator.
- **Revisions.** Statistics Canada may revise recent-year estimates; the
  published files are regenerated from the source on each build.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run sohbc fetch statcan_wds
uv run sohbc build mortality_rates_bc mortality_age_specific_bc
```

The tidy dataset is published at `data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv`
(all ages and age groups, by sex), with the age-standardised series — one
row per year and sex — at
`data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv` (standard
population weights in `data/reference/who_standard_population.csv`). The
headline trend tests are at `data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json`
and `data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json`, and
the per-sex tests at
`data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json`.
